attacks.claim: Self-update trusts a minisign key compiled into the binary, but the plan never describes key rotation or compromise recovery. If the signing key leaks, every installed kvx will accept malicious updates from the same key, and the only fix is shipping a new binary that users must already have installed manually.
attacks.evidence: "The minisign public key is compiled into the binary; the archive is rejected unless the signature verifies. The same key already signs our releases today"

attacks.claim: The update path downloads and replaces the executable with no described check that the signed archive's version matches the requested tag, and no downgrade protection. An attacker who can replay an older validly-signed release (e.g. vulnerable v2.6.2) via a tampered release listing or the --version flag could force users back onto a known-vulnerable build.
attacks.evidence: "kvx self-update [--check] [--version vX.Y.Z]" and "Queries the GitHub Releases API for the latest non-prerelease tag"

attacks.claim: The plan does not state that the signature is verified over the archive before extraction, or that archive extraction guards against path traversal (zip-slip) when writing the temp file.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: archive extraction and path-sanitisation details

attacks.claim: The install ID is a persistent random identifier that is linkable across all telemetry events over time, and the plan does not define its deletion or rotation. Combined with the consent prompt's ambiguous wording, this is personal-linkable data collected from users who opted in without a documented retention limit.
attacks.evidence: "a random install ID generated locally (not derived from hostname, user, or MAC)"

attacks.claim: Consent wording says 'anonymous' yet the payload includes a stable install ID plus OS/arch and version, which is quasi-identifying; the 'anonymous' label overstates the guarantee.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats (command name, backend type, kvx version, OS/arch)?"

attacks.claim: Telemetry is opt-in but the prompt is shown only on first interactive run after upgrade, and users who never answer are never re-asked; there is no statement about whether an install ID is generated before consent is given.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: whether install ID is generated before the consent answer

attacks.claim: Update and telemetry depend on GitHub Releases API and the project's single donated VPS; there is no self-hosted mirror or documented way for enterprises to point self-update or telemetry at internal infrastructure.
attacks.evidence: "on the project's existing donated VPS"

attacks.claim: The telemetry collector is a single ~150-line service on one donated VPS with no described capacity, rate limiting, or backpressure. At ~14,000 weekly downloads, even modest opt-in rates produce daily POST volume that the collector and its host are never sized against, and a traffic spike or outage silently drops data with no alerting.
attacks.evidence: "a ~150-line Go service on the project's existing donated VPS, writing daily aggregate counts only"

attacks.claim: The update check is a GET to GitHub's API from every user's startup once per 24 h; for a large install base this is an unbounded external request load on the GitHub API that the plan does not budget against unauthenticated rate limits.
attacks.evidence: "at most once per 24 h, a single stderr line"

attacks.claim: The plan says no new paid infrastructure, but the cost of bandwidth on the donated VPS for full archive downloads (<12 MB each, for every self-update and rollback) and the collector's storage are not estimated.
attacks.evidence: "full archives are < 12 MB"

attacks.claim: The atomic rename and kvx.prev rollback are described, but there is no handling for the case where the rename succeeds and the new binary crashes on first run, or where kvx.prev is overwritten by a second update before the user notices a regression. Users can be left with no working binary.
attacks.evidence: "The previous binary is kept as kvx.prev; kvx self-update --rollback swaps them back."

attacks.claim: Telemetry transport failures are silently dropped with no local counter or observability, so the maintainers' stated goal of prioritising backends can be skewed by systematic drop-off (e.g. corporate proxies) without anyone noticing.
attacks.evidence: "failures are dropped, never retried in the foreground"

attacks.claim: The telemetry collector writes raw events and aggregates to a donated VPS with no described retention policy or deletion path for already-collected data, and the plan provides no way to purge a user's install ID from aggregates. Opt-out after the fact does not remove data already sent.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention policy and deletion/purge mechanism for install IDs and aggregates

attacks.claim: The success metric (share on latest minor >= 75%, from 59%) conflicts with the motivation section, which states 41% of downloads are on versions <= v2.6.2, implying 59% on newer versions; but the metric is about the latest minor and the baseline is not defined against the same window, so the target cannot be evaluated as written.
attacks.evidence: "41% of release-asset downloads 60 days later were still for versions <= v2.6.2" versus "share of downloads on the latest minor version >= 75% (from 59%)"

attacks.claim: Telemetry 'once per day' transport and the 24 h update-check cadence are not reconciled with the 'at most once' phrasing, leaving unclear whether a missed day is sent on next run.
attacks.evidence: "at most one POST per day, fire-and-forget with 2 s timeout"

attacks.claim: The motivating claim that the 41% stale-download figure is caused by slow upgrades is unsupported: GitHub download counts include CI, mirrors, Homebrew bottles and package-repo mirrors, and are not per-installed-user, so self-update may not move this number.
attacks.evidence: "(GitHub release download counts, tallied per asset)"

attacks.claim: The 14,000 weekly downloads figure and the 78 thumbs-up count are asserted without source or date, and the plan's success measure depends on them.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: source/date for ~14,000 weekly downloads and 78 combined thumbs-up

attacks.claim: Startup notice on every 24 h interval adds a stderr line to interactive commands, and the telemetry consent prompt adds an additional first-run interruption; neither is measured for friction.
attacks.evidence: "Startup notice: at most once per 24 h, a single stderr line"

attacks.claim: The consent prompt relies on a '[y/N]' text convention and no alternate non-TTY-friendly or screen-reader-specific flow is described; the prompt is text-only, which is acceptable but not analysed.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats (command name, backend type, kvx version, OS/arch)? [y/N]"

attacks.claim: Telemetry collection from EU/UK users with a stable install ID may require a documented lawful basis and data processing notice under GDPR; the plan defers this to docs/telemetry.md without specifying the legal basis or processing record.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: legal basis and data processing description beyond docs/telemetry.md

attacks.claim: Package-manager detection by path prefix (Homebrew Cellar, dpkg/rpm ownership) is brittle across distros and custom prefixes, and the plan has no test for non-standard prefixes or Linuxbrew paths.
attacks.evidence: "if the binary path is under a Homebrew Cellar or is owned by the dpkg/rpm database"

attacks.claim: The timeline puts the full telemetry collector and docs in week 3 with a one-week RC, leaving no slack for the 2-maintainer team to validate the consent flow end-to-end before release.
attacks.evidence: "Week 3: collector service, docs/telemetry.md, release notes, v2.8.0-rc1 for 1 week, then v2.8.0."
